title: Incomer, going-away, driven and overhead
summary: Targets that come towards you, fly away from you or pass over your head: how to recognise them and what many coaches suggest.

body.html: An incomer flies towards you, often from a far trap or a tower, and usually drops as it comes. It can seem to slow down and hang in the air. That tempts you to stop the gun and aim at it like a rifle, a common cause of a miss. It is usually shot while it is still in front of you, before it is overhead. At the moment you fire, the barrels may hide the target (“blot it out”). Many coaches let this happen on such targets: it is usually intended, not a mistake.

A going-away target leaves from near or behind you and flies away. It needs little lead to the side, but it gets small fast and often rises or drops. So you mostly need to shoot a little above it if it rises, or a little below it if it drops, and timing matters: do not wait. In Compak® Sporting a going-away target over side BC is compulsory. It may come from a trench in front of the stations or from a tower behind them, at least 4 m above the stations.

A driven target is an incomer that passes over your head, like a pheasant pushed by beaters. Many coaches teach it like this. Find it with your eyes early and start moving the gun with it. Bring the gun up from behind the target and through it, fire at the moment the barrels hide it, and keep the gun moving.

An overhead from behind comes over your back and goes away. It is seen late, so many coaches suggest looking back for it before you call. Bring the gun to your shoulder (the mount) as it passes over. Fire as the end of the barrels reaches its front edge, and keep the gun moving after the shot (follow-through).
“Incoming” and “going away” always describe the target relative to the shooter.

notes.html: Careful: French “en battue” (Italian “in battuta”) means driven game, not the battue target.

phrases.speaker: coach
phrases.en: Take it out in front, before it gets on top of you.
phrases.meaning: Break the incomer while it is still in front, not when it is overhead.

phrases.speaker: coach
phrases.en: Blot it out and keep swinging.
phrases.meaning: Let the barrels cover the target at the shot and do not stop the gun.

phrases.speaker: coach
phrases.en: Don't wait on the going-away — it's getting smaller.
phrases.meaning: Shoot the going-away target promptly, because it is quickly getting further away.

phrases.speaker: coach
phrases.en: It comes from behind you — look back for it early.
phrases.meaning: It is an overhead from behind; turn the eyes towards it before calling.

key_points.html: Incomer: comes towards the shooter, usually dropping; take it in front.
Going-away: little lead to the side; shoot a little above it if it rises, below if it drops; do not wait.
Driven: an incomer over the head; swing through from behind and cover it.
Overhead from behind: look back early, mount with it, follow through.
A going-away target is compulsory on a Compak® Sporting field.

quiz.q: The coach says: “Blot it out.” What should the shooter do?

options.text: Wipe the lenses of the safety glasses
Let the barrels cover the target at the shot
Wait until the target disappears from view
Shoot only at the falling pieces

quiz.explain: On incomers, driven and rising targets the gun often covers the clay at the moment of the shot; the coach asks for exactly that.

quiz.q: Why should a going-away target not be left too long?

options.text: It quickly gets further away and smaller
The rules allow only three seconds
It always turns into a crosser
The referee calls No Bird after the peak

quiz.explain: A going-away target gains distance fast, so the longer you wait, the harder it becomes. Three seconds is the release time, not a shooting limit.

quiz.q: What makes a driven target different from an ordinary incomer?

options.text: It comes from behind the shooter
It passes over the shooter's head
It is thrown only in Compak® Sporting

quiz.explain: Driven means an incomer that comes over the head, like driven game. A target coming from behind is an overhead from behind.
